added_claim_errors: "Part D is 63 days" confuses the penalty threshold with the enrollment deadline: the key specifies 2 full months after coverage ends.
"If you don't have 40 quarters, Part A carries a premium" ignores qualification through a spouse's work history.
"Covering little your plan doesn't already cover" is unsupported without knowing the employer plan's benefits.
"Six-month Medigap open enrollment ... (in most states)" misleadingly qualifies a federal protection for this 65-year-old.
"You'll need" an HR letter overstates a requirement; the key specifies CMS-L564, not a mandatory separate letter.
"If you're not on Social Security, nothing happens automatically" is too broad: Railroad Retirement beneficiaries can also be automatically enrolled (assessed from my own knowledge).

reasons: Both immediately correct the coworker's premise, but B gives a more focused checklist and avoids A's incorrect Part D deadline and categorical Part A eligibility claim. A supplies useful premium and Medigap details; its annual premium rounding checks out because $202.90 × 12 = $2,434.80. Both omit the IEP-ending exception, complete HSA timing instructions, and the retirement application routes and forms. B wins narrowly because its safer, shorter guidance outweighs its missing cost and Medigap specifics.
